A cubic meter is a cube so big that you could sit inside it.
Say each cube in here is 1 cubic centimeter.
One layer is 3 times 2 equals 6, and there are 2 layers, so that is 12.
And we say the box is 12 cubic centimeters, not just 12.
Now, which size cube should you pick?
Small things take small cubes, cubic centimeters or cubic inches.
Big things take big cubes, cubic feet or cubic meters.
One last thing to watch.
Don't use square units for the space inside.
Squares cover a flat floor. It takes cubes to fill a box.
If I just point and say up there, near the middle, that could be lots of different spots.
Your friend would hunt around for ages.
What you need is two numbers, and an order to read them in.
Go across first, then up.
3 across and 5 up is the point (3, 5).
Always start at 0, down in the corner.
Now walk along the bottom, and stop when you are right under point A.
Count as you go, 1, 2, 3.
Now, from right there, head straight up.
Keep going until you land on point A.
Count them with me, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
So we made two moves, and we have two numbers.
The one across goes first, and the one up goes second.
That gives us point A at (3, 5).
Here is the mix-up to watch for.
Don't write the number up first.
(5, 3) means 5 across and 3 up, and that is a whole different spot.
Look at all the spots on this grid.
The pair (4, 2) tells you exactly which one to use.
But only if you make the two moves in the right order.
To find (4, 2), start at 0.
Go 4 across, then 2 up.
Put the dot there.
Put your finger on 0, right in the corner.
The first number is 4, so slide along the bottom.
One, two, three, four. Stop.
The second number is 2, so now go straight up from where you stopped.
One, two. Stop again.
Now put your dot right where you stopped.
That one spot is (4, 2), and there is only one of them on the whole grid.
The flag goes there.
Don't go up 4 and across 2.
That lands you on (2, 4), which is a different spot altogether.
You might guess that Leo is always 4 dollars ahead.
It is a fair guess, but it is not what happens.
Leo pulls further ahead every single week.
So we have to write both lists out and look.
Follow each rule one step at a time.
Then line the two patterns up and compare the numbers in each column.
Let's do Mia first.
Her rule is start at 0, then add 2 every week.
One week at a time, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.
Now Leo. Same start, but his rule adds 6 every week.
Now look straight down each column.
2 and 6. 4 and 12. 6 and 18.
Every number in Leo's row is 3 times the number in Mia's.
Now, back to that first guess.
Don't say Leo always has 4 more.
6 minus 2 is 4, sure, but 12 minus 4 is 8.
The thing that stays the same every week is 3 times as much.
Here is the trouble.
A grid will not take a list of numbers.
Every dot needs two numbers, one across, and one up.
Take the two numbers in each column as a pair.
The top number goes across, the bottom number goes up.
Read straight down each column.
0 and 0. 1 and 2. 2 and 4. 3 and 6.
Each column gives you one pair.
Now take those pairs over to the grid.
Go across by the top number, then up by the bottom number.
Put a dot there, and do the same for all four.
Now look at what those dots did.
They line up perfectly, climbing as they go right.
Every 1 step across, they go 2 steps up.
Don't put the bottom number first.
Pattern A is the one that goes across.
(2, 1) is nowhere near the same dot as (1, 2).
You could count every single step from the bench to the tree.
That works, but on a big grid it takes a long time.
And it is so easy to lose count halfway along.
When two points share one number, they are on the same straight line.
Subtract the other two numbers.
First, read both points off the grid.
A is at (2, 3), and B is at (7, 3).
Now look at the second number of each one.
Both are 3 up, so they sit on the same straight line going across.
Now the two numbers that are different.
Those are the ones across, 2 and 7.
Take the smaller away from the bigger, and you get 5.
Let's check it the slow way, just this once.
Count the steps along the line from A to B.
One, two, three, four, five. They really are 5 units apart.
Don't subtract the numbers that match.
3 minus 3 is 0, and A and B are certainly not 0 apart.
You could trace the street with your finger and count the blocks.
But look how busy this map is.
It is easy to skip a block, or to count the same one twice.
On a map grid, every place has a pair, across first, then up.
Along one straight street, subtract to count the blocks.
Same move as always, go across, then up.
The school is at (2, 3).
And the park is at (2, 8), straight above it.
Both of them are 2 across, so one straight street joins them.
Now subtract the numbers that are different, the ones going up.
8 minus 3 equals 5, so the park is 5 blocks away.
Now let me turn it around. What is at (6, 1)?
Go 6 across, then 1 up.
The library is right there.
Don't count the corners you pass.
Count the blocks between them.
From 3 up to 8 up is 5 blocks, not 6.
Make the pieces the same size first. Then add how many pieces you have.

Add the wholes, then add the pieces. If the pieces make a whole, trade them for 1 more whole.
Compare each fraction to one half. Two parts more than one half make more than 1, and two parts less than one half make less than 1.
Draw the story as bars. Then decide, put the parts together, or find the gap.
Each X is one thing, measured by the number under it. Read the numbers, then add or take away.
A fraction is a share. 3 divided by 4 is the same as three fourths.

Put the rectangle on one square meter. Count the pieces it covers out of all the pieces.
Times a number less than 1 gives less than you started with. Times more than 1 gives more.
Sharing a piece makes smaller pieces. Cut it up, then see how big one share is in the whole.
Draw the story first. Are you taking part of an amount, or counting how many pieces fit?
The third place after the point is thousandths. So 47 thousandths is 0.047.
Line up the places and compare from the left. The first place that is different decides.
Find the two numbers it sits between, then pick the closer one. Halfway or past it rounds up.
Line up the points, so each place sits under the same place. Then add like whole numbers and bring the point straight down.
Line up the points and fill any empty place with a 0. Then take away like whole numbers.
Break the decimal into wholes, tenths and hundredths. Multiply each part, then add.
Multiply by 10 and every digit moves one place left. Divide by 10 and every digit moves one place right, 100 is two places and 1,000 is three.
Count the decimal in tenths. Share the tenths equally, then write the answer with a point again.
To change to a smaller unit, multiply, because you need more of them. To change to a bigger unit, divide, because you need fewer.
Volume is how many cubes fill the inside. Find one layer, then multiply by how many layers.
Multiply the length, the width and the height. That gives the volume of a box.
Cut the sides into halves and count the small tiles. It takes 4 small tiles to make 1 square foot.
A shape can belong to more than one family. If it follows a family’s rule, that name fits it too.
